facts.text: The Caspian tern is the world's largest species of tern.
facts.quote: The Caspian tern (Hydroprogne caspia) is the world's largest species of tern, with a subcosmopolitan but scattered distribution.

facts.text: It has a long thick red-orange bill with a small black tip and black legs.
facts.quote: Adult birds have black legs, and a long thick red-orange bill with a small black tip.

facts.text: Unlike many other terns, the Caspian tern keeps its black cap in winter, though with some white streaking on the forehead.
facts.quote: In winter, the black cap is still present (unlike many other terns), but with some white streaking on the forehead.

facts.text: It catches fish by hovering high over the water and then plunging, and may fly up to 60 km from its breeding colony to do so.
facts.quote: They may fly up to 60 km (37 mi) from the breeding colony to catch fish; they often fish on freshwater lakes as well as at sea.

facts.text: Besides fish, it occasionally eats large insects, the young and eggs of other birds, and rodents.
facts.quote: They also occasionally eat large insects, the young and eggs of other birds and rodents.

facts.text: Chicks vary in plumage from pale creamy to darker grey-brown, which helps parents recognize their own young back at the colony.
facts.quote: The chicks are variable in plumage pattern, from pale creamy to darker grey-brown; this variation assists adults in recognizing their own chicks when returning to the colony from feeding trips.

facts.text: In 2016, a pair bred in northwestern Alaska, 600 km further north than any previous North American breeding record, part of a trend linked to global warming.
facts.quote: In 2016, a pair of Caspian terns bred successfully in the Cape Krusenstern National Monument in northwestern Alaska, 600 km further north than any previous North American breeding record.

facts.text: The global population is about 50,000 pairs, but the Baltic Sea population is declining and of conservation concern.
facts.quote: The global population is about 50,000 pairs; numbers in most regions are stable, but the Baltic Sea population (1400–1475 pairs in the early 1990s) is declining and of conservation concern.
